clue.text: Dad and, yes, German mum wear the trousers, or jacket. What a game!

parts.note: pa is an informal word for one's father
ja is the German word for yes
ma is an informal word for one's mother

explanation.surface: A family row over who rules the household, with Mum in charge and a German voice approving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wear the trousers' suggests a domineering mother, but the trousers and jacket are nightwear; 'What a game!' is just an exclamation rounding off the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Either half of a set of nightclothes, the trousers or the top, can be called by this name in the singular.

clue.text: Wine had Loquacity when -canalized

parts.note: port is a fortified wine from Portugal
to have loquacity, talkativeness, is to speak, so this gives a past tense of speaking

explanation.surface: A drinker became chatty once the drink had been channelled into him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Canalized' looks like a jokey word for drunk, but it points to the Suez Canal, at whose Mediterranean end this Egyptian city stands.
explanation.definitionFit: The Egyptian city sits at the northern entrance of the Suez Canal, so it is the place you reach when the route becomes a canal.

clue.text: Swift to a Star, for one

definitions.text: Swift to a Star, for one

parts.words: Swift to a Star, for one
parts.note: Jonathan Swift's letters to Stella, whose name means star, were published as a diary-like record of his days

explanation.surface: A speedy athlete's progress toward stardom.
explanation.walkthrough: Swift is the author, not 'fast', and Star translates Stella, the name he gave Esther Johnson; his letters to her are known as the Journal to Stella.
explanation.definitionFit: Swift's letters to Stella form a daily record, the kind of diary that title names.

clue.text: "Egoist" doctor, medium-weight in Greater Manchester

parts.note: something medium sits in the middle
a ton is a unit of weight

explanation.surface: A self-centred physician of average build working in the north of England.
explanation.walkthrough: Dr Middleton is the scholarly father of Clara in George Meredith's novel The Egoist; the same name is also a town in Greater Manchester, which the clue's last words point to.
explanation.definitionFit: In Meredith's novel The Egoist the heroine's father is the Reverend Dr Middleton, a classical scholar.

clue.text: Girl chums artists find .colourful ?.

definitions.meaning: read as pal plus the feminine ending -ette, female pals
the boards on which painters mix their colours are full of colour

explanation.surface: Some young women friends who think painters are colourful characters.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading is a joke: PAL plus the feminine diminutive -ETTE makes girl pals.
explanation.definitionFit: A painter's mixing board is daubed with many pigments, and a female pal could jokingly be a pal-ette.

clue.text: Wrong, dessert to serve on Concorde

definitions.text: Wrong, dessert to serve on Concorde

parts.words: Wrong, dessert to serve on Concorde
parts.note: concord means harmony, and the fruit of Greek myth that set goddesses quarrelling is the wrong thing to offer at a peaceful gathering

explanation.surface: An airline catering blunder: the wrong pudding served on a supersonic flight.
explanation.walkthrough: Concorde is concord, harmony; the golden fruit Eris threw among the goddesses caused the quarrel leading to the Trojan War, so it would spoil any harmony.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names any cause of strife, after the golden fruit marked 'for the fairest' in Greek myth.

clue.text: Amid the clatter, great success !

indicators.note: amid means in the middle of, so the letters sit inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A triumph greeted by a great din.
explanation.definitionFit: A brilliant success, with dazzling effect, is a borrowing from French.

clue.text: Still life of willow rising over the' water abroad.

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece written over another comes first
in a down clue rising means the word is read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: cricket bats are made of willow, so willow stands for a bat
l'eau is French for the water

explanation.surface: A painting of a willow tree reaching up over a foreign river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still life' looks like a genre of painting, but here it means a motionless scene, as in a tableau vivant.
explanation.definitionFit: A group of people posed motionless to represent a scene is a living picture, a frozen piece of life.

clue.text: All of a one without warning.

definitions.meaning: the one word that completes the phrase all of a ..., meaning abruptly
something that happens with no notice is abrupt

explanation.surface: Everything happening at once and unannounced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' stands for the missing word of a familiar phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: An abrupt event comes unannounced, as in the phrase all of a ..., meaning abruptly.

clue.text: Fate of a tram. more obviously than of a bus

definitions.text: Fate of a tram. more obviously than of a bus

parts.words: Fate of a tram. more obviously than of a bus
parts.note: a tram on rails has its end point fixed in advance far more plainly than a bus that can change route

explanation.surface: A gloomy thought about how public transport comes to its end.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as PRE-DESTINATION: a tram's destination is fixed by its rails beforehand.
explanation.definitionFit: Fate decided in advance, and also a destination fixed beforehand, as for a vehicle on rails.

clue.text: Puckish journey

parts.note: Puck in A Midsummer Night's Dream promises to put a girdle round about the earth in forty minutes

explanation.surface: A mischievous trip.
explanation.walkthrough: Puckish looks like 'mischievous', but refers to Shakespeare's Puck and his journey circling the earth and coming back.
explanation.definitionFit: A journey out and back again, like Puck's circuit of the globe, ends where it began.

clue.text: Look, "sleeping accommodation with hanging sections

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look or behold
a bed is somewhere to sleep

explanation.surface: An advert pointing out a sleeping space with curtains hanging round it.
explanation.definitionFit: Having rounded projecting parts, like an earlobe or leaf divisions that hang down.

clue.text: Chosen to chant and was followed

parts.note: to chant is to sing
one who led was followed by others

explanation.surface: A choir member picked to lead the singing and others came after.
explanation.definitionFit: Picked out from a group, as one selected for special notice.

clue.text: Listen' to the current of the Exe when far out

indicators.note: listen to tells you to go by the sound of the words, not their spelling

parts.note: the Exe is a river in Devon, so its current is the Exe stream

explanation.surface: Hearing the flow of a Devon river at the far end of its course.
explanation.walkthrough: The Exe is a river in Devon, south-west England; 'Exe stream' run together sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something far out is at the outermost limit, utmost or most remote.

clue.text: Hired to Yeats at Innis-free?

definitions.meaning: read as two words, ..., meaning rented out
Yeats wrote of the Lake Isle of Innisfree, a small island in Lough Gill

explanation.surface: A poet renting a cabin on an Irish lake.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as IS LET for 'hired'. Yeats's poem The Lake Isle of Innisfree describes building a small cabin on the island.
explanation.definitionFit: A rented thing is let out; and Innisfree is a tiny lake island in Yeats's poem.

clue.text: Painter of. Nocturnes in French cabaret act?

definitions.meaning: the painter Whistler called many of his night scenes Nocturnes, and his name means one who whistles
a French word for a whistling performer on stage

explanation.surface: An artist known for night scenes performing in a Paris nightclub.
explanation.walkthrough: The painter is James McNeill Whistler; the answer is French for a whistler.
explanation.definitionFit: A French word for one who whistles, as a music-hall turn, which also names the painter Whistler.

clue.text: Proverbially shed, on late literary-work

parts.note: writing done late at night is proverbially said to smell of the oil that lit it

explanation.surface: Light that is said to fall on authors burning the midnight oil.
explanation.walkthrough: Laboured writing is said to 'smell of the lamp', from scholars working through the night by lamp.
explanation.definitionFit: The glow by which scholars once worked through the night is what proverbially falls on their writing.

clue.text: More than just cross — a girl grows weary

parts.note: Sal is a short form of the girl's name Sally
to grow weary is to tire

explanation.surface: Someone moves from annoyance to exhaustion, more than merely angry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like 'angry', but it is the shape: these are diagonal crosses like that of St Andrew, in more than one.
explanation.definitionFit: A St Andrew's cross is a diagonal heraldic cross, and the plural means more than one of them.

clue.text: What a bind, Iris, to be upset by port

indicators.note: upset means knocked over and jumbled, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone complains that a friend called Iris is annoyed by a glass of fortified wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' looks like the wine but is the Adriatic seaport in southern Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: An Italian seaport on the Adriatic, in Apulia.

clue.text: This spoon, last thing a pest makes off with

definitions.meaning: a style of antique spoon with a ridge running down the back of the bowl

definitions.text: last thing a pest makes off with
definitions.meaning: the rodent pest's rear appendage is the last part of it to vanish as it scurries off

explanation.surface: A rodent running off with the family silver.
explanation.walkthrough: The spoon takes its name from the tapering ridge on the back of its bowl.
explanation.definitionFit: A spoon with a tapering ridge under the bowl; and the hindmost part of a scurrying rodent.

clue.text: In last night of Christmas she causes road collision in backing

definitions.text: In last night of Christmas she

indicators.note: backing means going in reverse, so the pieces are read backwards

parts.note: the A1 is Britain's longest numbered road, its 1 read as the letter I
a ram is a collision, a hit made by driving into something

explanation.surface: A Twelfth Night guest who crashes her car while reversing.
explanation.walkthrough: Twelfth Night is the last night of the Christmas season; in Shakespeare's play she is Olivia's maid. The A1 is the main road from London to Edinburgh.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's Twelfth Night, named after the last night of Christmas, she is Olivia's witty gentlewoman.

clue.text: Rose might lose her head 'to an …

definitions.text: Rose might lose her head 'to an

parts.words: Rose might lose her head 'to an
parts.note: a climbing rose of this kind, with its first letter dropped, becomes the answer to the next clue

explanation.surface: A girl called Rose falls for a passing admirer.
explanation.walkthrough: Rose looks like a girl's name but is the flower; drop the first letter of the answer to get the answer to 22, which completes the sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: A climbing or trailing variety of rose bush, also a word for a wanderer.

clue.text: … easy-going chap

parts.note: a man who walks at an unhurried pace, easy-going in a literal sense

explanation.surface: A relaxed fellow, continuing the previous sentence.
explanation.walkthrough: The dots continue clue 21: the rose's answer loses its head to become this one.
explanation.definitionFit: One who strolls at a leisurely pace goes easily on foot.

clue.text: Swagman's command dancing partner

parts.note: in Australian slang a swagman's bundle has a girl's name, and carrying it on the road is called waltzing it

explanation.surface: An Australian tramp orders his dance partner about.
explanation.walkthrough: A swagman is an Australian itinerant; his swag is personified as a girl, and 'waltzing' it, as in the famous song, makes her a dancing partner.
explanation.definitionFit: Australian slang for a tramp's bundle, which he 'waltzes' along the road, as in the song.

clue.text: Lady has article translated in the island

indicators.note: the English article a is turned into its French counterpart un inside the word

explanation.surface: A woman's essay is translated while she stays on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: The article A in LADY becomes UN, its French translation. Lundy is an island in the Bristol Channel.
explanation.definitionFit: An island in the Bristol Channel, off the coast of Devon.

clue.text: Hatchet-burying smoke

parts.note: burying the hatchet means making peace, and Native Americans sealed peace by sharing a ceremonial pipe

explanation.surface: Smoke rising after a quarrel is settled.
explanation.walkthrough: To bury the hatchet is to make peace; the smoke is from a ceremonial pipe.
explanation.definitionFit: A Native American ceremonial tobacco pipe, smoked to seal peace.

clue.text: Mead of the Senior Service, we are given to understand

parts.note: mead is a poetic word for meadow, as is lea
the Royal Navy, abbreviated RN, is called the Senior Service as the oldest British armed service

explanation.surface: A drink brewed by the Royal Navy, so we hear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mead' looks like the honey drink but is a meadow. The Royal Navy is known in Britain as the Senior Service.
explanation.definitionFit: To come to know something, as we do when we are told of it.

clue.text: Sort of verb to describe Holmes's young helpers

definitions.meaning: a verb that does not follow the regular pattern of endings
Sherlock Holmes's band of street urchins were called the Baker Street ...

explanation.surface: A grammar lesson about the street boys who helped Sherlock Holmes.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb with nonstandard forms; and Holmes's street urchins were the Baker Street gang of that name.

clue.text: Partlet keeping up good work with the BBC?

definitions.meaning: Partlet is a traditional name for a hen, from Chaucer's Pertelote, and her good work is producing eggs again and again
broadcasters pass on programmes by transmitting them on

explanation.surface: A hen staying productive while appearing on the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: Partlet is the hen in Chaucer's Nun's Priest's Tale. Split the answer as RE-LAYING, laying eggs again.
explanation.definitionFit: Passing on a broadcast by retransmitting it; and a hen laying eggs once more.

clue.text: Gazes at old starlings in flight, say

definitions.meaning: stare is an old dialect word for a starling, so a flock of them flying is a group of these birds

explanation.surface: Someone watching a murmuration of starlings in the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: Looks at fixedly; and an old dialect name for starlings in the plural.
